observedProblem: Repeat use fell from 5 of 8 eligible lawyers in the onboarding period to 1 of 8 two periods later, although 7 of 8 had activated after training.

supportingEvidence.summary: Repeat users 5, then 2, then 1 of 8 eligible lawyers across the first three reporting periods.

Median 167.5 active minutes per signed-off issues list (median of per-task totals, 10 accepted of 12 attempts) against a team estimate of 140 minutes without the tool; 5 of 10 sampled results went back for a second correction round.
In three shadowed reviews the lawyer rebuilt the output into the team's own clause checklist before reviewing it.

hypothesis: The output order does not match the team's review checklist, so lawyers restructure it by hand and the tool saves no time. Training is not the constraint.
action: Map the workflow output to the team's 14-point supplier checklist, add a reviewer sign-off step, and run two supervised review clinics with the Corporate group.

expectedResult.metric: Repeat users and median minutes to a signed-off issues list
expectedResult.target: At least 6 of 8 eligible lawyers as repeat users and a median below 100 minutes

followUpObservations.summary: First follow-up period: repeat users 6 of 8; sampled median 86 minutes (9 results).
Second follow-up period: repeat users 6 of 8; rework on 2 of 11 sampled results.
Third complete period: repeat users 7 of 8; follow-up sample median 90 active minutes per accepted result (30 accepted of 31 attempts); 2 quality failures.

outcome.rationale: Both targets were met in three consecutive complete reporting periods.
confounders: German clause-library release on 11 May, inside the follow-up window
No comparison group; eight eligible users

observedProblem: In the German-language legal summary workflow, 25 of 36 draft outputs were verified and 4 were blocked at review; 7 were neither verified nor blocked.

supportingEvidence.summary: 25 of 36 draft outputs verified; 4 blocked at review.

hypothesis: Reviewers are unsure which outputs need a second reader, so sign-off stalls.
action: One 60-minute session on the reviewer sign-off step with the Employment group.

expectedResult.target: At least 30 of 36 comparable draft outputs verified in the next reporting period

observedProblem: Employment has no checklist-mapped review workflow. The General Counsel asked for the Corporate playbook to be extended.

supportingEvidence.summary: Request recorded in the review meeting of 20 July.

hypothesis: The checklist mapping transfers to employment-contract review if the checklist is rebuilt with the Employment lead. This is untested.
action: Rebuild the checklist with the Employment lead and pilot with three lawyers for one reporting period before any seat increase.

expectedResult.metric: Repeat users in the Employment pilot and median minutes to a signed-off result
expectedResult.target: All three pilot lawyers as repeat users and a median below the group's own pre-pilot sample

observedProblem: Fewer than half of started drafting runs reached a partner-accepted draft: 81 of 184 in the first two reporting periods.

supportingEvidence.summary: Completion 41 of 88 and 40 of 96 started runs.
The Innovation Lead attributed the gap to prompting skill among associates.

hypothesis: Associates lack prompting fluency; a refresher will raise completion.

expectedResult.metric: Completion rate of started drafting runs
expectedResult.target: At least 60 of 100 started runs reach a partner-accepted draft

followUpObservations.summary: Activity rose to 134 started runs; 43 reached an accepted draft (32%).
141 started, 45 completed. Median active time per accepted draft rose from 222.5 to 260 minutes; rework on 14 of 26 sampled drafts.

outcome.rationale: Activity increased after the training while completion fell and correction time rose. The prompting-skill hypothesis is not supported.
confounders: Two large transactions closed in June

observedProblem: Correction is the largest single step on the way to an accepted draft: a median of 110 correction minutes against a median task total of 260. Partners rewrite the negotiated clauses of agent drafts.

supportingEvidence.summary: Median 260 active minutes per accepted draft after the training against 222.5 before; 26 of 32 attempts accepted against 24 of 27; quality failures on 9 of 26 sampled drafts against 5 of 24.
Correction categories reviewed on 26 sampled drafts with two supervising partners: 17 concerned negotiated risk-allocation clauses.

hypothesis: The workflow scope is too broad. Negotiated risk-allocation clauses need partner judgment early; the agent helps on definitions, schedules and boilerplate.
action: Narrow the agent scope to definitions, schedules and boilerplate for a six-week trial with one deal team; partners draft risk-allocation clauses directly.

expectedResult.metric: Median minutes to a partner-accepted draft and rework rate
expectedResult.target: Median below 180 minutes and rework on fewer than 8 of 26 comparable drafts

observedProblem: In the GDPR DPA review workflow, 22 of 39 draft outputs were verified and 9 were blocked at review.

supportingEvidence.summary: Practice leads said they re-check every cited provision by hand.

hypothesis: Reviewers do not trust citations because the verification step is not part of their review routine.
action: Citation-verification clinic with the Corporate and Employment practice leads, then a shared verification checklist.

expectedResult.target: At least 30 of 39 comparable draft outputs verified

observedProblem: Weekly active users fell from 20 to 8 of 40 licensed seats over five weeks.
hypothesis: Partners do not rely on output without source verification, and no active sponsor sets expectations for the group.
action: Sponsor meeting with the managing partner's office, then supervised use for two Litigation partners.

expectedResult.target: At least 9 of 20 licensed Litigation seats active per week
